title: The House With the Belvedere

full_text:
In Damascus lived an enlightened young architect named Tariq who was commissioned by an affluent merchant to design a grand mansion in the garden district beside the Barada river.

Tariq constructed a magnificent belvedere—a high, octagonal observation pavilion crowned with a cedar dome, featuring arched windows on all eight sides to catch the mountain breezes and afford panoramic views of the orchards and minarets.

However, an elderly neighbor who lived in the adjacent modest cottage complained to the Chief Magistrate, fearing that the high belvedere would overlook his private courtyard and disturb the domestic seclusion of his family.

Rather than disputing the complaint with legal arguments, Tariq invited the neighbor and the magistrate to the belvedere.

He demonstrated his ingenious architectural solution: the lower half of each window was fitted with intricately carved wooden mashrabiya screens, angled with such geometric subtlety that the viewers within could look out upon the snow-capped mountains and river cascades, while the neighboring courtyards below were completely shielded from view!

Furthermore, Tariq had constructed a marble fountain upon the terrace whose soothing murmur masked all household sounds, and trained fragrant climbing roses across the trellis to provide sweet scent to both houses.

The elderly neighbor was enchanted by the delicate consideration of the architect: 'You have not only built a window to the mountains; you have built an arbor of peace between neighbors!'

The merchant rewarded Tariq with a thousand dinars, and the belvedere became a celebrated model of architectural courtesy throughout Damascus.
moral: Art and architecture should open windows to the beauty of nature and harmony with one's neighbors.
